How to predict the brightest saturated stars: what we learned and what to try next¶

2026-10-23, rewritten 2026-10-24 with simpler language and more pictures.

The story in one paragraph. Our first model restores saturated pixels well for ordinary stars, but when we test it on the brightest stars its predictions are up to 10 times too low. We asked three questions, each studied by a separate agent and then checked: (1) was that test fair? (2) can we ask the model a different, easier question? (3) would a different kind of model, such as a neural network, do better? The short answers: the test was unfair and we built a better one; for three quarters of the NIRCam pixels that matter most, the detector's very first read already gives the answer; and for the rest, a model with a straight-line part does better than the current tree model. A neural network helps for the same reason, but it adds risk and gains nothing over the simpler choice.

Words used in this notebook¶

word meaning here
level (sat_level) how many of the 5 reads (groups) the pixel got before it saturated. Level 4: four good reads. Level 0: already saturated in the first read group, so the pipeline has no value at all. These are the pixels we most need to restore.
label the "correct answer" we train on: the pixel's flux according to a PSF fit of its star (the fit uses the unsaturated pixels around the core).
training set / test set we teach the model with the training set and grade it on the test set. The model never sees the test set while it learns, like exam questions a student has not seen.
hold-out another name for the test set: the stars we "hold out" of training to grade the model with.
cross-validation split the stars into 5 groups; train on 4, test on the 5th; repeat 5 times so that every star is tested once.
extrapolation predicting for stars brighter than any star the model learned from.
dex a factor, on a log scale. 0.1 dex = x1.26 (26%), 0.2 dex = x1.6, 0.3 dex = x2, 1 dex = x10.
bias the typical (median) error. -0.3 dex means the predictions are typically 2 times too low.
scatter how widely the errors spread: half the width of the middle 68% of the errors. A scatter of 0.1 dex means most predictions are within about 26% of the truth (after removing the bias).
ZEROFRAME the very first read of the detector, 10.7 s after it was reset (section 4).
A-hard, A-soft, B, C kinds of NIRCam level-0 pixels (section 4).

import numpy as np

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.lines import Line2D
from matplotlib.patches import Patch
from astropy.table import Table
import xgboost as xgb
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge
from sklearn.neural_network import MLPRegressor
from scipy.ndimage import binary_dilation

BLUE, ORANGE, AQUA, YELLOW = '#2a78d6', '#eb6834', '#1baf7a', '#eda100'   # categorical slots 1-4, in fixed order
INK, MUTED, GREY = '#0b0b0b', '#52514e', '#b5b4ae'
plt.rcParams.update({'axes.spines.top': False, 'axes.spines.right': False, 'axes.grid': True, 'grid.color': '#e6e5e0',
                     'grid.linewidth': 0.6, 'axes.edgecolor': GREY, 'axes.labelcolor': INK, 'xtick.color': MUTED,
                     'ytick.color': MUTED, 'lines.linewidth': 2, 'font.size': 11, 'axes.titlesize': 12,
                     'axes.titleweight': 'bold', 'legend.frameon': False, 'figure.dpi': 110})
D = '/orange/adamginsburg/w51/TaehwaYoo/w51_sat_recover'
half_width = lambda s: (np.percentile(s, 84) - np.percentile(s, 16)) / 2
dec = lambda s: s.map(lambda v: v.decode() if isinstance(v, bytes) else v)

def end_label(ax, x, y, text):
    # name the line at its right end, in text ink (colour alone never carries identity)
    ax.annotate(text, (x[-1], y[-1]), xytext=(6, 0), textcoords='offset points', va='center', fontsize=10, color=INK)

def end_labels(ax, items, gap=0.07):
    # items: (x, y, text) at the right end of each line (log2 x axis); labels pushed apart so they never overlap
    lo, hi = ax.get_ylim()
    items = sorted(items, key=lambda it: it[1])
    ys = [it[1] for it in items]
    for i in range(1, len(ys)):
        ys[i] = max(ys[i], ys[i - 1] + gap * (hi - lo))
    for (x, y, text), yl in zip(items, ys):
        ax.text(x * 1.1, yl, text, va='center', fontsize=10, color=INK)

1. The problem in one picture¶

Each point is one level-0 NIRCam pixel. Horizontal: its label (the answer). Vertical: what the model predicted. A perfect model puts every point on the dashed line.

  • Left: the model is tested on stars similar to the ones it learned from (cross-validation). The points follow the line.
  • Right: the brightest 20% of stars in each filter are held out, and the model learns only from the fainter 80%. The points form a flat band: whatever the true brightness, the model predicts about the same value, up to 10 times too low.

2. What "hold-out" means, and why tree models go flat¶

2.1 Two ways to test a model¶

A model is graded on stars it did not learn from. Which stars we hold out decides what the grade means.

  • Brightest stars held out (left). Train on the fainter stars (blue), test on the brightest ones (orange). This asks: can the model predict stars brighter than anything it has seen? That is extrapolation, the case we care about for the brightest stars in W51.
  • Cross-validation (right). Five rounds; in each round a different fifth of the stars (orange) is tested and the rest (blue) are used for training. The stars are picked at random, so the test stars look like the training stars. This asks: does the model work for stars like the ones it learned from?

The first model passed the right-hand test (section 1, left panel) and failed the left-hand one (section 1, right panel).

2.2 Why a tree model goes flat beyond what it has seen¶

A toy problem with one input x (think: how bright the star is) and one answer y (think: the pixel's flux). We train each model on x < 2 (grey area) and ask it to predict up to x = 3.

In [4]:
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
x = rng.uniform(0, 2, 2000)
y = x + 0.3 * np.sin(3 * x) + rng.normal(0, 0.05, x.size)   # a rising trend plus some wiggle
grid = np.linspace(0, 3, 300)

class LinearPlusTrees:
    # a straight line for the trend, trees for what the line leaves over
    def fit(self, X, y):
        self.lin = Ridge(alpha=1e-3).fit(X, y)
        self.tree = xgb.XGBRegressor(n_estimators=300, max_depth=4, learning_rate=0.05).fit(X, y - self.lin.predict(X))
        return self
    def predict(self, X):
        return self.lin.predict(X) + self.tree.predict(X)

models = [('trees (XGBoost, our first model)', BLUE, '-', xgb.XGBRegressor(n_estimators=300, max_depth=4, learning_rate=0.05)),
          ('straight line (linear)', ORANGE, '--', Ridge(alpha=1e-3)),
          ('line + trees', AQUA, '-', LinearPlusTrees()),
          ('neural network', YELLOW, '-.', MLPRegressor(hidden_layer_sizes=(64, 64), max_iter=2000, random_state=0))]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 5.5))
ax.axvspan(0, 2, color='#f0efec', zorder=0)
ax.text(1, 3.0, 'training range: the model sees these', ha='center', color=MUTED)
ax.text(2.5, 3.0, 'beyond: never seen', ha='center', color=MUTED)
ax.scatter(x[::10], y[::10], s=6, c=GREY, zorder=1)
ax.plot(grid, grid + 0.3 * np.sin(3 * grid), ':', color=INK, lw=1.5)
end_label(ax, grid, grid + 0.3 * np.sin(3 * grid), 'truth')
for name, c, ls, m in models:
    p = m.fit(x[:, None], y).predict(grid[:, None])
    ax.plot(grid, p, ls, color=c, label=name)
for seed in (1, 2, 3):   # the same network started from other random numbers
    nn = MLPRegressor(hidden_layer_sizes=(64, 64), max_iter=2000, random_state=seed).fit(x[:, None], y)
    ax.plot(grid, nn.predict(grid[:, None]), '-.', color=YELLOW, lw=0.8)
ax.set_xlim(0, 3.3); ax.set_xlabel('x  (like: how bright the star is)'); ax.set_ylabel('y  (like: the pixel flux)')
ax.legend(loc='lower right')
Out[4]:
<matplotlib.legend.Legend at 0x14e2abc715d0>

What the picture shows.

  • Trees (blue) copy the wiggle inside the grey area well, then stay flat beyond it. A tree model is a big lookup table: for an input it has never seen, it returns the answer of the nearest thing it has seen. This is exactly the flat band in section 1.
  • A straight line (orange, dashed) keeps rising beyond the grey area, but misses the wiggle inside it.
  • Line + trees (aqua) gets both: the line carries the trend into the unseen area, the trees add the wiggle.
  • A neural network (yellow) also keeps rising: it is built from many small straight pieces and continues along the last one. The thin yellow lines are the same network started from other random numbers: inside the grey area they agree; beyond it they spread apart. So a network does extrapolate, but where it goes depends on chance.

No model gets the wiggle beyond x = 2 right, because nothing in the training data shows it.

3. Question 1: was the "brightest 20%" test fair?¶

3.1 What it left for the model to learn from¶

Level-0 pixels exist almost only in bright stars (a faint star does not saturate in the first read). So when we held out the brightest 20% of the stars, almost all level-0 pixels went to the test side. What was left on the training side was mostly junk: a single bad pixel (a hot pixel or a cosmic ray) that the pipeline flags together with its 8 neighbours, which looks like a tiny 3x3 saturated "star". Their labels are wrong by factors of 5 to 500. (Junk here: saturated regions of 12 pixels or fewer with level-0 pixels, and star-exposures whose level-0 labels disagree with the ZEROFRAME of section 4 by more than x3.)

In [5]:
PQ = pd.read_parquet(f'{D}/nextml/verify/band_test_pred.parquet')   # same rows as training_v4.fits; junk and band per row

test = n0.pred_orig.notna()   # rows of the brightest-20% stars
cnt = pd.DataFrame({'good': [(~test & ~n0.junk).sum(), (test & ~n0.junk).sum()],
                    'junk': [(~test & n0.junk).sum(), (test & n0.junk).sum()]},
                   index=['training side\n(fainter 80% of stars)', 'test side\n(brightest 20%)'])

ax.barh(cnt.index, cnt.good, color=BLUE, edgecolor='white', linewidth=2)
ax.barh(cnt.index, cnt.junk, left=cnt.good, color=GREY, hatch='//', edgecolor='white', linewidth=2)
for i, (g, j) in enumerate(zip(cnt.good, cnt.junk)):
    ax.text(g + j + 400, i, f'{g:,} good + {j:,} junk', va='center', color=INK)
ax.set_xlim(0, cnt.sum(axis=1).max() * 1.35); ax.invert_yaxis()
ax.set_xlabel('NIRCam level-0 pixels'); ax.grid(axis='y', visible=False)
ax.legend(handles=[Patch(fc=BLUE, label='good level-0 pixels'), Patch(fc=GREY, hatch='//', ec='white', label='junk (3x3 hot pixels, cosmic rays, ...)')],
          loc='upper center', bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.32), ncol=2)
plt.tight_layout()
cnt
Out[5]:
good junk
training side\n(fainter 80% of stars) 2 2809
test side\n(brightest 20%) 43360 1498

The model had essentially no good level-0 examples to learn from. So this test mostly measured "a model that never saw a real level-0 pixel", and says little about extrapolation.

3.2 A fairer test: brightness bands¶

The verifier agent built a test that removes the junk and still asks the extrapolation question, step by step:

  1. In each filter, take F1 = the brightness of a fairly faint star that already has level-0 pixels (the 25th percentile of such stars).
  2. Train on stars up to F1.
  3. Test on stars in bands: 1-2 x F1, 2-4 x F1, 4-8 x F1, and so on up to 32 x F1. The band tells how far beyond the training stars we ask the model to go (x2, x4, ..., x32).
  4. A star seen in several filters goes into the band of its brightest filter, so the same star is never on both sides.

This way we see how the error grows as we go further beyond the training stars, instead of one number for "all bright stars".

In [6]:
nb = n0[~n0.junk].groupby('band').star_id.nunique()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 2.6))
segs = [(2 ** -2, 1, BLUE, f'training\n{nb[0]} stars')] + [(2 ** (k - 1), 2 ** k, ORANGE, f'x{2 ** k}\n{nb[k]} stars') for k in range(1, 6)]
for x0, x1, c, t in segs:
    ax.barh(0, x1 - x0, left=x0, height=0.5, color=c, edgecolor='white', linewidth=3)
    ax.text(np.sqrt(x0 * x1), -0.42, t, ha='center', va='top', color=INK, fontsize=10)
ax.set_xscale('log', base=2)
ax.set_xticks([2 ** k for k in range(-2, 6)], ['', '', 'F1', '2 F1', '4 F1', '8 F1', '16 F1', '32 F1'])
ax.set_ylim(-1.3, 0.5); ax.set_yticks([]); ax.grid(False); ax.spines['left'].set_visible(False)
ax.set_xlabel('star brightness (stars with good NIRCam level-0 pixels)')
ax.set_title('Brightness bands: train on the blue stars, test on each orange band separately')
plt.tight_layout()

3.3 The first model on the fair test¶

The same XGBoost as before, trained on the blue stars only, graded on each band.

In [7]:
bt = pd.read_csv(f'{D}/nextml/verify/band_test.csv')
r = bt[(bt.split == 'band<=0') & (bt.inst == 'NIRCam') & (bt.l0_type == 'all')].sort_values('factor')
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4.8))
ax.axhline(0, color=GREY, lw=1)
ax.plot(r.factor, r.scat_vs_label, 'o-', color=BLUE, ms=8); end_label(ax, r.factor.values, r.scat_vs_label.values, 'scatter (spread)')
ax.plot(r.factor, r.bias_vs_label, 's--', color=ORANGE, ms=8); end_label(ax, r.factor.values, r.bias_vs_label.values, 'bias (typical offset)')

ax.set_xscale('log', base=2); ax.set_xticks(r.factor, [f'x{int(f)}' for f in r.factor])
ax.set_xlim(1.7, 60); ax.set_xlabel('how far beyond the training stars'); ax.set_ylabel('error (dex)')

Out[7]:
Text(0.5, 1.0, 'XGBoost, NIRCam level-0 pixels, graded against the labels')

Reading it. Up to x2 beyond the training stars, the first model is fine: the scatter (0.12 dex) equals the uncertainty of the labels, and there is almost no bias. From x4 on, the error grows: at x16-x32 the scatter is about 0.44 dex (a factor 2.7) and the predictions are typically 0.2-0.3 dex (x1.6-x2) too low. So the dramatic "x10 too low" of section 1 came mostly from the unfair test; the real extrapolation problem is smaller, but it is there.

4. A second ruler that needs no PSF: the ZEROFRAME¶

To grade predictions for the brightest stars we need to know their true flux. The labels come from a PSF fit. Is there another measurement to check them with?

4.1 What the ZEROFRAME is¶

NIRCam reads the detector many times while the light collects; the signal in a pixel grows like a straight line in time until it reaches the saturation level, and then stays there. The pipeline uses groups (averages of 2 reads). The very first read, 10.7 s after the reset, is also saved separately: the ZEROFRAME. For a very bright pixel this first read can be below saturation even though group 0 is already saturated.

In [8]:
TF = 10.737                                   # s between reads (NIRCam SHALLOW2)
reads = TF * np.arange(1, 27)
groups = [TF * np.array([5 * g + 1, 5 * g + 2]) for g in range(5)]   # each group = 2 reads, then 3 skipped
SAT = 50000                                   # schematic saturation level (DN)
pix = [('ordinary bright pixel (level 2)', 420, BLUE), ('A-soft: first read OK, group 0 saturated', 3200, AQUA),
       ('A-hard: saturated even in the first read', 9000, ORANGE)]
t = np.linspace(0, 250, 600)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 5.5))
ax.axhline(SAT, color=INK, lw=1, xmax=250 / 285); ax.text(253, SAT, 'saturation', va='center', color=INK)
for g, tt in enumerate(groups):
    ax.axvspan(tt[0] - 2, tt[1] + 2, color='#f0efec', zorder=0)
    ax.text(tt.mean(), -4500, f'group {g}', ha='center', color=MUTED, fontsize=9)
for name, rate, c in pix:
    s = np.minimum(rate * t, SAT)
    ax.plot(t, s, color=c, label=name)
    for g, tt in enumerate(groups):
        v = np.minimum(rate * tt, SAT).mean()
        ok = rate * tt[1] < SAT
        ax.plot(tt.mean(), v, 'o', ms=9, color=c, mfc=c if ok else 'white', mew=2)
    zf = min(rate * TF, SAT)
    ax.plot(TF, zf, '*', ms=16, color=c, mec=INK if rate * TF < SAT else c, mfc=c if rate * TF < SAT else 'white')
ax.annotate('ZEROFRAME:\nthe first read, 10.7 s', (TF, 3200 * TF), xytext=(40, 22000), color=INK,
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='->', color=MUTED))
ax.set_xlim(0, 285); ax.set_ylim(-7000, 58000)
ax.set_xlabel('time since reset (s)'); ax.set_ylabel('signal in the pixel (DN)')
ax.legend(handles=ax.get_legend_handles_labels()[0] + [Line2D([], [], marker='o', ls='', color=MUTED, ms=8, label='usable read'),
          Line2D([], [], marker='o', ls='', color=MUTED, mfc='white', mew=2, ms=8, label='group containing a saturated read'),
          Line2D([], [], marker='*', ls='', color=MUTED, ms=13, label='first read (ZEROFRAME); hollow = saturated')], loc='center right')
ax.set_title('Schematic: three pixels of different brightness')
Out[8]:
Text(0.5, 1.0, 'Schematic: three pixels of different brightness')

The four kinds of NIRCam level-0 pixels, in these terms:

kind first read (ZEROFRAME) what we know
A-soft below saturation the flux, measured directly from the first read
B below saturation (group 0 is flagged by a rule for averaged reads) the same
C below saturation (flagged only because a neighbour saturated) the same
A-hard saturated only a floor: the pixel is at least as bright as a pixel that saturates within 10.7 s

MIRI has no ZEROFRAME (each MIRI group is a single read), so this ruler exists for NIRCam only.

4.2 Does the ZEROFRAME agree with the labels?¶

To compare them we convert the ZEROFRAME to the same units as the labels with one number per exposure, taken from pixels where both are good. Then we compare on level-2 pixels, where the labels are reliable (the fit sees those pixels).

In [9]:
t = Table.read(f'{D}/model_v4/training_v4.fits')
T = pd.DataFrame({c: np.asarray(t[c]).astype(float) for c in
                  ['label', 'cal_value', 'zeroframe_rate', 'sat_level', 'sat_area', 'psf_star_flux', 'star_id', 'source_index']})
for c in ('inst', 'filter', 'l0_type', 'file'):
    T[c] = dec(pd.Series(np.asarray(t[c])))
assert len(PQ) == len(T)
T['junk'] = PQ.junk.values
n = T[T.inst == 'NIRCam'].copy()
ok = n.sat_level.isin([3, 4]) & (n.cal_value > 0) & (n.zeroframe_rate > 0)
conv = (n[ok].cal_value / n[ok].zeroframe_rate).groupby(n[ok].file).median()   # DN/s -> MJy/sr, one per exposure
n['zf'] = n.zeroframe_rate * n.file.map(conv)
l2 = n[(n.sat_level == 2) & (n.zf > 0)]
ratio = np.log10(l2.label / l2.zf)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.2, 5.6))
lo, hi = np.percentile(np.log10(l2.zf), [0.5, 99.5])
ax.hexbin(np.log10(l2.zf), np.log10(l2.label), gridsize=60, bins='log', cmap='Blues', mincnt=1, extent=(lo, hi, lo, hi))
ax.plot([lo, hi], [lo, hi], '--', color=INK, lw=1)
ax.set_xlabel('flux from the ZEROFRAME (log10 MJy/sr)'); ax.set_ylabel('label from the PSF fit (log10 MJy/sr)')
ax.set_title(f'Level-2 pixels: label / ZEROFRAME = {10 ** ratio.median():.3f}\nscatter {half_width(ratio):.3f} dex ({len(l2):,} pixels)')
Out[9]:
Text(0.5, 1.0, 'Level-2 pixels: label / ZEROFRAME = 0.998\nscatter 0.069 dex (150,911 pixels)')

They agree: typical ratio 1.00, with a scatter of 0.07 dex (17%). So for A-soft, B and C pixels the ZEROFRAME is a second, independent ruler, and it needs no PSF model at all.

4.3 The labels of the very brightest stars are too low¶

Now the same comparison for level-0 pixels (A-soft and B), as a function of how bright the star is within its filter. Percentile 0.9 means "brighter than 90% of the stars in this filter".

In [10]:
pct = n.groupby(['filter', 'star_id']).psf_star_flux.median().groupby(level=0).rank(pct=True)
c = n[(n.sat_level == 0) & ~n.junk & n.l0_type.isin(['A-soft', 'B']) & (n.zf > 0)].copy()
c['pct'] = [pct.get((f, s)) for f, s in zip(c['filter'], c.star_id)]
c['wave'] = np.where(c['filter'].str[1:4].astype(int) > 250, 'long wave (F335M-F480M)', 'short wave (F140M-F212N)')
c['r'] = np.log10(c.label / c.zf)
edges = np.array([0.9, 0.925, 0.95, 0.975, 1.0])   # level-0 A-soft/B pixels occur almost only above the 90th percentile
c['bin'] = pd.cut(c.pct, edges)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 5))
ax.axhline(0, color=INK, lw=1); ax.text(0.902, 0.01, 'label = ZEROFRAME', color=INK, va='bottom', fontsize=9)
for (w, g), col, mk in zip(c.groupby('wave'), [ORANGE, BLUE], ['s', 'o']):
    s = g.groupby('bin', observed=True).r
    mid = np.array([iv.mid for iv in s.median().index])
    ax.fill_between(mid, s.quantile(0.16), s.quantile(0.84), color=col, alpha=0.15, lw=0)
    ax.plot(mid, s.median(), marker=mk, color=col, ms=8)
    end_label(ax, mid, s.median().values, w)
ax.axvspan(0.95, 1.0, color='#f0efec', zorder=0); ax.text(0.975, 0.17, 'brightest 5%', ha='center', color=MUTED)
ax.set_xlim(0.9, 1.05); ax.set_ylim(-0.55, 0.22)
ax.set_xlabel('star brightness percentile within its filter'); ax.set_ylabel('log10( label / ZEROFRAME )  (dex)')
ax.set_title('NIRCam level-0 pixels (A-soft, B): line = median, band = middle 68%\n(each point: 12-50 stars)')
Out[10]:
Text(0.5, 1.0, 'NIRCam level-0 pixels (A-soft, B): line = median, band = middle 68%\n(each point: 12-50 stars)')

Reading it. Level-0 pixels of these kinds occur almost only in stars brighter than 90% of the others. Up to the 95th percentile the labels agree with the ZEROFRAME. Above it they fall below: in long wave from the 95th percentile on, in short wave mostly in the top 2.5%. Over the whole brightest 5%, the labels are typically 0.09 dex (x0.8) too low in short wave and 0.23 dex (x0.6) in long wave; for the brightest 2.5% alone, 0.16 and 0.27 dex. The total flux of these stars is fine (it repeats between dithers to 3%); what goes wrong is how the PSF fit spreads that flux over the saturated core. A likely reason is that the brightest long-wave objects are not single clean stars: they saturate a larger area than one star of their brightness could (close pairs, or a star on bright nebulosity).

What this means.

  1. At the bright end, a prediction that disagrees with the label is not necessarily wrong. From now on we grade against the ZEROFRAME where it exists (A-soft, B, C), and check the floor for A-hard pixels.
  2. For three quarters of the NIRCam level-0 pixels (section 7), we can simply use the ZEROFRAME instead of predicting.

5. Question 2: ask the model an easier question (a "reference")¶

5.1 The idea¶

A tree model cannot answer above the values it has seen (section 2.2). So change the question so that bright and faint stars give the same kind of answer.

An everyday example. You want to guess how tall a building is from a photo. Its height in the photo (in pixels) depends on how far away you stood, so a guess learned from photos taken close up fails for photos taken from far away. But if a person stands next to the building, you can ask instead: how many people tall is it? That number does not depend on the distance. The person is a reference: something you can measure in the same photo that scales the same way.

Here. The pixel's flux depends on how bright the star is. A reference is something we can measure in the same image, without a PSF fit, that also scales with the star. The model then predicts

flux / reference ("how many references bright is this pixel")

which is similar for faint and bright stars, and we multiply by the measured reference at the end. The extrapolation is done by the measured reference, and the model only learns the part that does not change with brightness.

A toy version: stars with a simple profile; the reference is the flux 4 pixels from the centre (outside the saturated core). Both models below are the same tree model with the same inputs; only the question differs.

In [11]:
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
logB = rng.uniform(0, 3, 400)                               # log10 star brightness
r = rng.uniform(0, 2.5, (400, 20))                          # 20 core pixels per star: distance from the centre (px)
prof = lambda r: -0.5 * (r / 1.2) ** 2 / np.log(10)        # log10 of the star's profile
logF = (logB[:, None] + prof(r) + rng.normal(0, 0.03, r.shape)).ravel()   # the pixel flux we want
log_ref = np.repeat(logB + prof(4.0) + rng.normal(0, 0.03, 400), 20)      # measured 4 px out: the reference
X = np.c_[log_ref, r.ravel()]
train = np.repeat(logB < 2, 20)
tree = lambda: xgb.XGBRegressor(n_estimators=300, max_depth=5, learning_rate=0.05)
p_flux = tree().fit(X[train], logF[train]).predict(X)
p_ratio = tree().fit(X[train], (logF - log_ref)[train]).predict(X) + log_ref
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 5.2), sharex=True, sharey=True)
for ax, p, title in zip(axes, [p_flux, p_ratio], ['Question: "what is the flux?"', 'Question: "how many references bright?"\n(answer x measured reference)']):
    ax.scatter(logF[train][::4], p[train][::4], s=5, color=BLUE, label='training stars')
    ax.scatter(logF[~train][::2], p[~train][::2], s=5, color=ORANGE, label='brighter stars, never seen')
    ax.plot([-1, 3.2], [-1, 3.2], '--', color=INK, lw=1)
    ax.set_title(title); ax.set_xlabel('true pixel flux (log)')
axes[0].set_ylabel('predicted pixel flux (log)'); axes[0].legend(loc='upper left', markerscale=3)
plt.tight_layout()

Left: the tree goes flat for the brighter stars, as before. Right: the same tree, asked for the ratio, is right for the brighter stars too, because the ratio does not depend on brightness and the measured reference carries the brightness.

5.2 The references we tried¶

The question is what to use as the "person next to the building". Three candidates, all measurable without a PSF fit:

In [12]:
yy, xx = np.mgrid[-14:15, -14:15]
img = 2e5 * (1 + (xx ** 2 + yy ** 2) / 2.2 ** 2) ** -2.5
sat = img > 2500
ring = binary_dilation(sat, iterations=3) & ~sat
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 6.5))
ax.imshow(np.log10(img), cmap='Greys', origin='lower', extent=(-14.5, 14.5, -14.5, 14.5))
over = np.zeros(img.shape + (4,))
over[sat] = (0.165, 0.47, 0.84, 0.75); over[ring] = (0.92, 0.41, 0.2, 0.75)
ax.imshow(over, origin='lower', extent=(-14.5, 14.5, -14.5, 14.5))
ax.add_patch(plt.Rectangle((1.5, 0.5), 1, 1, fill=False, ec=YELLOW, lw=3))
ax.annotate('saturated core:\nthe pixels we want', (0, -2), xytext=(-13.5, -12), color=INK, arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='->', color=INK))
ax.annotate('ring 1-3 px outside the core:\nthe "ring" reference', (5, 5), xytext=(1, 11.5), color=INK, arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='->', color=INK))
ax.annotate("one core pixel: its own first read\n(ZEROFRAME) or unsaturated groups:\nthe \"pixel rate\" reference", (2.5, 1.2),
            xytext=(4, -12.5), color=INK, arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='->', color=INK))
ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([]); ax.grid(False); ax.set_title('A saturated star (schematic)')
Out[12]:
Text(0.5, 1.0, 'A saturated star (schematic)')
reference what it is what the model then predicts
ring the typical (median) flux in a ring 1-3 pixels outside the saturated core how much brighter the pixel is than the ring
pixel rate the pixel's own measured rate: from its unsaturated groups, or from the ZEROFRAME (section 4). For A-hard pixels only a lower limit a small correction to a measurement
star scale an estimate of the star's total brightness from the size of the saturated area and the ring the pixel's share of the star
combination the pixel rate where the pixel has a real measurement, the star scale where it has none (A-hard) either of the above

5.3 The ring turned out to be a weak reference¶

A good reference grows in step with the star: twice the star, twice the reference (the dashed line, slope 1). The ring grows much more slowly.

In [13]:
R = Table.read(f'{D}/nextml/targets/ring_ref.fits').to_pandas()
R['file'] = dec(R['file'])
S = T.groupby(['file', 'source_index']).agg(F=('psf_star_flux', 'first'), filt=('filter', 'first')).reset_index()
RS = S.merge(R[['file', 'source_index', 'ring_med']], on=['file', 'source_index'])
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 5))
for ax, f in zip(axes, ['F182M', 'F410M']):
    g = RS[(RS.filt == f) & (RS.ring_med > 0) & (RS.F > 0)]
    lx, ly = np.log10(g.F), np.log10(g.ring_med)
    ax.hexbin(lx, ly, gridsize=45, bins='log', cmap='Blues', mincnt=1)
    k, b0 = np.polyfit(lx, ly, 1)
    xs = np.array([lx.min(), lx.max()])
    ax.plot(xs, k * xs + b0, color=ORANGE); end_label(ax, xs, k * xs + b0, f'measured: slope {k:.2f}')
    ax.plot(xs, xs - np.median(lx) + np.median(ly), '--', color=INK, lw=1); end_label(ax, xs, xs - np.median(lx) + np.median(ly), 'ideal: slope 1')
    ax.set_xlim(xs[0] - 0.1, xs[1] + 1.1)
    ax.set_title(f'{f}: {len(g):,} star-exposures'); ax.set_xlabel('star brightness from the PSF fit (log)')
axes[0].set_ylabel('ring flux (log MJy/sr)')
plt.tight_layout()

The ring sits at the edge of the saturated core, and the core grows with the star. So the ring moves outward as the star gets brighter, and its flux stays close to the saturation level: it measures the saturation level more than the star. Dividing by it removes only part of the brightness.

5.4 Results on the fair test¶

Left: C pixels graded against the ZEROFRAME (the independent ruler). Right: A-hard pixels, where only the floor is known: the fraction of predictions that are impossible (more than 1.5 times below the floor). Lower is better in both.

In [14]:
sb = pd.read_csv(f'{D}/nextml/targets/band/summary_band.csv')
sb = sb[sb.inst == 'NIRCam']
cands = [('base', 'flux (first model)', BLUE, 'o-'), ('rate_ramp', 'pixel rate', ORANGE, 's--'),
         ('combo', 'combination', AQUA, 'D-'), ('ring_feat', 'ring', YELLOW, '^-.')]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 4.8))
labs = [[], []]
for cand, name, col, st in cands:
    for k, (grp, val) in enumerate([('L0_C', 'scat_vs_zf'), ('L0_A-hard', 'pred_below_floor_x1p5')]):
        a = sb[(sb.cand == cand) & (sb.group == grp)].sort_values('factor')
        axes[k].plot(a.factor, a[val], st, color=col, ms=7); labs[k].append((a.factor.iloc[-1], a[val].iloc[-1], name))
axes[1].plot(a.factor, a.label_below_floor_x1p5, ':', color=MUTED); labs[1].append((a.factor.iloc[-1], a.label_below_floor_x1p5.iloc[-1], 'the labels themselves'))
for ax, l in zip(axes, labs):
    end_labels(ax, l)
axes[0].set_ylabel('scatter vs ZEROFRAME (dex)'); axes[0].set_title('C pixels: error against the ZEROFRAME')
axes[1].set_ylabel('fraction below floor / 1.5'); axes[1].set_title('A-hard pixels: impossible predictions')
for ax in axes:
    ax.set_xscale('log', base=2); ax.set_xticks([2, 4, 8, 16, 32], ['x2', 'x4', 'x8', 'x16', 'x32'])
    ax.set_xlim(1.7, 110); ax.set_xlabel('how far beyond the training stars')
plt.tight_layout()

Reading it.

  • Pixel rate (orange) is the best reference for pixels that have a measurement (left): at x32 the error against the ZEROFRAME is 0.13 dex, against 0.37 for the first model. It works because the measured rate already is nearly the answer; the model only fine-tunes it.
  • For A-hard pixels the pixel rate is only a lower limit, so it fails there (right: 75% impossible predictions at x32).
  • The combination (aqua) keeps A-hard predictions possible (21% below the floor at x32, against 69% for the first model and 44% for the labels themselves).
  • The ring (yellow) helps less, as section 5.3 suggests.
  • None of the references makes things worse for stars like the training stars (cross-validation error 0.138-0.149 dex for all, first model 0.141).

6. Question 3: a different kind of model, including neural networks¶

Same question as the first model ("what is the flux?"), same inputs, different kinds of models:

model in plain words beyond the training stars
XGBoost (first model) many small decision trees: a large lookup table stays flat
linear a straight-line formula in the (log) inputs keeps following the trend
line + trees (lin_xgbq) a straight line for the trend, trees for the details follows the trend, with details
neural network (mlp_skip) layers of simple units (3 layers of 256, 256, 128) plus a direct straight-line path from inputs to output follows the straight-line path
In [15]:
bm = pd.read_csv(f'{D}/nextml/models/band_models_all.csv')
bm = bm[bm.inst == 'NIRCam']
mods = [('xgb', 'XGBoost (first model)', BLUE, 'o-'), ('ridge', 'linear', ORANGE, 's--'),
        ('lin_xgbq', 'line + trees', AQUA, 'D-'), ('mlp_skip', 'neural network', YELLOW, '^-.')]
panels = [('all', 'scat_vs_label', 'All level-0 pixels:\nscatter vs the labels (dex)'),
          ('C', 'scat_vs_zf', 'C pixels:\nscatter vs the ZEROFRAME (dex)'),
          ('A-hard', 'pred_below_floor_x1p5', 'A-hard pixels:\nfraction below floor / 1.5')]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(17, 4.8))
lab = bt[(bt.split == 'band<=0') & (bt.inst == 'NIRCam') & (bt.l0_type == 'A-hard')].sort_values('factor')
for k, (ax, (typ, val, title)) in enumerate(zip(axes, panels)):
    l = []
    for m, name, col, st in mods:
        a = bm[(bm.model == m) & (bm.l0_type == typ)].sort_values('factor')
        ax.plot(a.factor, a[val], st, color=col, ms=7); l.append((a.factor.iloc[-1], a[val].iloc[-1], name))
    if k == 2:
        ax.plot(lab.factor, lab.label_below_floor_x1p5, ':', color=MUTED); l.append((lab.factor.iloc[-1], lab.label_below_floor_x1p5.iloc[-1], 'labels themselves'))
    ax.set_title(title); ax.set_xscale('log', base=2); ax.set_xticks([2, 4, 8, 16, 32], ['x2', 'x4', 'x8', 'x16', 'x32'])
    ax.set_xlim(1.7, 120); ax.set_xlabel('how far beyond the training stars')
    end_labels(ax, l)
plt.tight_layout()

Reading it.

  • Left and middle: every model with a straight-line part (linear, line + trees, neural network) stays accurate much further than XGBoost. Against the ZEROFRAME (middle) the difference is large: at x16 the linear model is off by 0.09 dex, XGBoost by 0.28. The reason: for these pixels the answer is simply proportional to the first read, which is a straight line, and a straight-line model continues it.
  • Right: A-hard pixels are hard for every model. All of them have about 0.5 dex scatter at x16-x32. The straight-line models make fewer impossible predictions (about 20% at x16-x32, XGBoost 50-80%).
  • The neural network is as good as line + trees for NIRCam. But (1) its gain comes from its built-in straight-line path, which the simpler models have too; (2) on MIRI it now and then predicts absurd values (off by up to 10^8); (3) where it goes beyond the data depends on chance (section 2.2); (4) it takes 30-120 s to train, against 1 s for the linear model. Without the straight-line path, the network does worse (75% impossible A-hard predictions).
  • Line + trees is also the best model for stars like the training stars (cross-validation): level-0 error 0.137 dex for NIRCam and 0.217 for MIRI, against 0.143 and 0.260 for XGBoost.
  • Its built-in error bars are too narrow: its "68%" range contains only 57% of the labels. They need to be widened before use.
  • MIRI has only 2-6 bright stars per band and no ZEROFRAME, so these results are mostly about NIRCam.

Other tools. lightgbm (not installed) has trees with a straight line inside every leaf, a natural fit for this problem, and is fast: worth trying. pysr (formula search) might find a simple formula for A-hard pixels. torch and catboost would add nothing over what we have.

7. Putting it together: which pixels need which method¶

In [16]:
cnt0 = n[(n.sat_level == 0) & ~n.junk].l0_type.value_counts()
meas = cnt0[['A-soft', 'B', 'C']].sum(); hard = cnt0['A-hard']
miri0 = ((T.inst == 'MIRI') & (T.sat_level == 0)).sum()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 2.8))
ax.barh(['NIRCam level 0', 'MIRI level 0'], [meas, 0], color=AQUA, edgecolor='white', linewidth=2, label='first read is fine: use the ZEROFRAME directly')
ax.barh(['NIRCam level 0', 'MIRI level 0'], [hard, miri0], left=[meas, 0], color=ORANGE, hatch='//', edgecolor='white', linewidth=2,
        label='no usable read: needs a model')
ax.text(meas / 2, 0, f'A-soft + B + C\n{meas:,} pixels ({meas / (meas + hard):.0%})', ha='center', va='center', color=INK, bbox=dict(fc='white', ec='none', alpha=0.85))
ax.text(meas + hard / 2, 0, f'A-hard\n{hard:,} ({hard / (meas + hard):.0%})', ha='center', va='center', color=INK, bbox=dict(fc='white', ec='none', alpha=0.85))
ax.text(miri0 + 400, 1, f'{miri0:,} pixels (no ZEROFRAME on MIRI)', va='center', color=INK)
ax.invert_yaxis(); ax.set_xlabel('pixels in the training set (junk removed)'); ax.grid(axis='y', visible=False)
ax.legend(loc='upper center', bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.35), ncol=2)
plt.tight_layout()

What the three studies say together.

  1. The "x10 too low" result came mostly from an unfair test. On a fair test the first model is fine up to x2 beyond its training stars, and its error grows after that.
  2. About three quarters of the NIRCam level-0 pixels do not need machine learning. Their first read (ZEROFRAME) measures them directly, and agrees with the labels to 0.07 dex where both can be trusted.
  3. The labels of the brightest 5% of stars are too low (by x0.8 in short wave, x0.6 in long wave). We need better labels before we can grade models at the very bright end.
  4. The real machine-learning problem is the A-hard pixels (NIRCam) and level 0 on MIRI: pixels with no usable read at all. For these, a model with a straight-line part (line + trees) works best of what we tried, but it is still off by about 0.5 dex for the brightest stars.
  5. Neural networks extrapolate thanks to their straight-line part. A simpler model with the same part does as well, with less risk. They stay an option for later.

Still open. For A-hard pixels we only know a floor, and the labels there are too low, so we cannot yet tell whether "combination" (which predicts higher) or "line + trees" (closer to the labels) is closer to the truth. For MIRI there is no second ruler, and only a handful of bright stars.

8. Next steps¶

# what why effort
1 Make the fair test the standard. Remove the junk from the training set, use the brightness bands as the extrapolation test, and grade against the ZEROFRAME and the floor as well as the labels. Every later result is graded with it. hours
2 Use the ZEROFRAME directly for NIRCam A-soft, B and C level-0 pixels, converted to MJy/sr with the pipeline's own per-pixel calibration. Restores three quarters of NIRCam level-0 pixels with no model, at about 0.07 dex. about a day
3 Better labels for the brightest stars: give the PSF fit the ZEROFRAME values of A-soft/B/C pixels as extra data, so only A-hard pixels stay unknown; rebuild the training set (v5). The fit then sees most of the core, which should remove the too-low labels and constrain the A-hard pixels from inside. half a day of code, about a day of cluster time
4 Line + trees for what is left (A-hard, MIRI level 0, NIRCam level 1). Compare the plain question with the "combination" reference, and try not allowing predictions below the floor. Best of the models tried, both for normal and for brighter stars. hours
5 Fix the error bars: widen the model's uncertainty range until it holds 68% of the test labels. Now it holds 57%. hours
6 Optional: try lightgbm; check the brightest stars with the narrow-band filters (F187N inside F182M, F405N inside F410M, 10 times fainter, so less saturated); a neural network with limits on its output. Extra checks; steps 1-5 do not depend on them. each a day or less

Two small bugs were fixed while preparing this: train_model.py lost the pixel y coordinate in its output (4d8f466), and assemble_training_set.py set the level-0 type code to "unknown" for most level-0 pixels (59b3c20; the scores change by less than 0.01 dex).

Decisions for you¶

  1. Restore NIRCam A-soft/B/C level-0 pixels from the ZEROFRAME directly, without a model (step 2)? Recommended.
  2. Give the PSF fit the ZEROFRAME pixels and rebuild the training set as v5 (step 3)? Recommended. The labels of many stars will change, so earlier checks of the labels would be repeated.
  3. Make the brightness-band test the standard extrapolation test, and drop the "brightest 20%" test (step 1)? Recommended.
  4. Replace XGBoost with line + trees, and keep neural networks for later (step 4)? Recommended.
  5. Install lightgbm (step 6)? Optional.
